course.name: Custom Nodes
course.description: Build, test, and ship your own WebAssembly node — from an empty folder to the Flow-Like catalog.
course.longDescription: Acme's support team needs a text normalizer the catalog doesn't have, so you'll build it: a real TypeScript Component Model node called normalize_text. You'll write the definition and run function line by line, prove them with mock-host tests, learn exactly what the sandbox does and doesn't enforce, and publish through the package registry — privately first, publicly when review says go. Along the way you'll internalize the contracts that keep packages alive: stable identifiers, per-node capabilities, manifest resource tiers, and release gates that catch breaking changes before your users do.

modules.title: Overview
modules.description: Choose the right extension model and read a complete node before you write one.

challenges.prompt: Acme wants normalize_text as a private integration, versioned on its own schedule, without forking Flow-Like. Which extension path fits?
challenges.explanation: A WASM package is the independently distributed, independently versioned path — exactly the private-integration case. A native Rust node is the tempting wrong answer: it would tie every whitespace fix to a Flow-Like build and release cycle. A shared function layer can't be installed as a catalog node at all, and the runtime only adapts between its two supported binary shapes — an arbitrary .wasm without the expected exports never becomes a node.

options.label: A WASM package built from a maintained Flow-Like template
A native Rust node compiled into a custom Flow-Like build
A shared function layer copied into each support board
Any WASM binary — the runtime adapts to whatever it exports

challenges.prompt: The support board wires normalize_text between the incoming request and the AI draft. Which statements about its pins are true?
challenges.explanation: Data pins carry values; execution pins carry control flow — that split is the whole pin model. A pure calculation can live on data pins alone (normalize_text takes exec pins only so the board can sequence it deliberately between steps). The label option is the classic trap: friendly labels can change freely — it's the internal pin names that saved boards store.

options.label: Data pins carry typed values such as strings and booleans
Execution pins decide which downstream path runs
Every node must expose execution pins, even pure calculations
Renaming a pin's friendly label breaks saved boards

challenges.prompt: Monday you rename the template's example node to normalize_text — nothing is published yet. Six months after shipping 0.1.0, a teammate renames the result pin to output. Which rename breaks saved boards?
challenges.explanation: Before anyone can save a board containing your node, internal names are free to change — that's why identity gets settled during setup. Afterward, boards have stored normalize_text and result, so the later rename severs those wires. The version-bump option is the trap: an updated package under the same ID must still honor the stored identifiers, which is exactly why renames are documented breaking changes rather than routine updates.

options.label: Only the later one — after publication, internal names live inside saved boards
Both — internal identifiers can never change once written in code
Neither — boards reconnect pins by friendly label
Neither — bumping the version number makes any rename safe

challenges.prompt: You install com.acme.text-tools. What is the authoritative source for the nodes Flow-Like shows in the catalog?
challenges.explanation: Discovery reads the compiled artifact: the runtime calls get_nodes and renders exactly what the binary declares. The manifest is the tempting wrong answer — it identifies and bounds the package (ID, version, memory, timeout) but registers no nodes. The publish wizard only displays what was already extracted from the binary, and the editor needs pins long before any first run.

options.label: The definitions the compiled binary exports through get_nodes
The package metadata section of flow-like.toml
The node list you confirmed in the publish wizard
Types recorded the first time each node executes

challenges.prompt: normalize_text needs no permissions — but Acme's next node will make HTTP calls and needs more memory. Which statements about where things are declared are correct?
challenges.explanation: Two layers, two jobs: capabilities are exported per node from code (addPermission("network:http")), while the manifest carries package-wide resource tiers. The manifest-grants option is the classic layering mistake — package-level network fields are not what the sandbox enforces per node. And zero capabilities still leaves the baseline contract intact: pins, outputs, and logging all work; only protected host services are gated.

options.label: Protected capabilities like network:http are declared on the node definition, in code
Memory and timeout tiers are set in flow-like.toml
Enabling HTTP in the manifest's network section is what grants a node HTTP access
A node with zero declared capabilities cannot read its input pins

challenges.prompt: A teammate refactors run() and deletes the ctx.activateExec("exec_out") line. Tests that only check outputs.result still pass. What happens on the support board?
challenges.explanation: Execution flow follows activated pins, not produced values — outputs without activateExec strand every downstream node, silently. ctx.success() is the tempting distractor: it reports that the run finished cleanly, but it activates nothing by itself. That's exactly why behavior tests should assert result.activateExec, not just output values. The catalog is unaffected either way: discovery reads the definition, which never changed.

options.label: result is computed, but nothing after normalize_text ever runs
The run fails with an explicit error
Nothing — ctx.success() activates the default execution pin
The node disappears from the catalog until it's fixed

modules.title: Your First Node
modules.description: Build the normalize_text package, prove its behavior at every layer, and release it safely.

challenges.prompt: In the run skeleton, which expression correctly fills TODO 3 — the value of the changed output?
challenges.explanation: changed should report whether normalization actually altered anything, and comparing the final result against the original input is the only expression that does. The option-based answers share one misconception: an enabled option doesn't mean it had an effect — already-clean text passes through untouched, and changed must say so. The length check misses pure case changes: lowercasing 'FIRE' changes the text but not its length.

options.label: result !== text
trim || lowercase
result.length !== text.length
true, whenever either option is enabled

challenges.prompt: mise run test is green, but mise run build fails during componentization. What's the correct read of the situation?
challenges.explanation: Unit tests execute your TypeScript source on a mock host; the build bundles and componentizes it — different pipelines, different failure classes. That's why both gates run on every loop. The mock-host option is tempting because mocks genuinely do hide things — but what they hide is enforcement and integration behavior, not bundler failures. No amount of extra test inputs fixes a dependency that componentize-js can't process.

options.label: Packaging is a separate gate — a dependency can be un-componentizable even when the logic is correct
The tests must be asserting the wrong things
The package ID in flow-like.toml is invalid
The mock host masked a logic bug; rerun the tests with more inputs

challenges.prompt: Once 0.1.0 is live in saved boards, which changes force a documented breaking change rather than a routine new version?
challenges.explanation: Saved boards store the package ID, the internal node name, and the pin names — changing any of them severs existing wires, so each is a breaking change that needs a documented migration. Friendly labels are the deliberate escape hatch: polish them any time. Resource tiers are the other tempting pick, but boards never store them — raising a tier changes limits, not identity.

options.label: Renaming the internal node name normalize_text
Renaming the result pin to output
Moving the package to a new package ID
Changing the friendly label from 'Normalize Text' to 'Clean Text'
Raising the memory tier from minimal to light

challenges.prompt: Your contract test asserts def.toDict().name === "normalize_text". Which real-world regression does that line catch?
challenges.explanation: toDict() pins down the serialized definition — the exact data Flow-Like extracts through get_nodes — so an innocent-looking rename fails the suite long before it can reach a registry. The other options are real failure classes, but they belong to other gates: behavior tests catch the changed bug, the component build catches bundling, and denial behavior needs the real sandbox or an integration fixture.

options.label: An accidental rename that would break every saved board after the next release
A wrong changed computation for whitespace-only input
A dependency that fails componentization
Unsafe behavior when a permission is denied

challenges.prompt: The whole Vitest suite is green on MockHostBridge. Which failures can that suite still be hiding?
challenges.explanation: The mock host runs your source logic — it never bundles it, never reads your permission list, and never replays an old board's stored wires. Those three failure classes live behind the build gate and the private-install gate. The whitespace case is the odd one out: if the suite explicitly covers it, the mock host is exactly the right tool to catch it — that's what unit tests are for.

options.label: A dependency that cannot be componentized
Real sandbox permission enforcement behaving differently than the mock
An existing saved board failing to resolve renamed identifiers
A wrong result for whitespace-only input that the suite explicitly covers

challenges.prompt: Which pieces of evidence belong in the release gate before 0.1.0 ships?
challenges.explanation: Three gates, three failure classes: source-level tests, packaging, and real-board discovery plus persistence. The fresh-board option is the subtle trap — one run in a scratch board skips persistence entirely; the check that matters is saving, closing, and reopening, and for later updates, loading a board saved under the previous version. Label spotting proves nothing contract-related: friendly labels aren't stored identifiers.

options.label: Contract, behavior, and permission-denial tests including boundary cases
A successful component build from reviewed source
A private install that runs inside a saved board — and still resolves after closing and reopening it
A successful run in one freshly created board
Confirmation that the catalog shows the friendly label you expected

challenges.prompt: The support board saved today wires normalize_text's result output into Send Reply. Which identifiers must every future version of the package keep for that wire to survive?
challenges.explanation: A saved board stores the chain package ID → node name → pin names; break any link and the wire dangles. Friendly labels are explicitly outside the contract — that's what makes them safe to polish at any time. Resource tiers are the tempting extra: they bound execution, but boards never store them, so tuning tiers is a routine version change.

options.label: The package ID com.acme.text-tools
The internal node name normalize_text
The internal pin names, including result
The friendly label 'Normalize Text'
The memory and timeout tiers in the manifest

challenges.prompt: Artifact 1: you merge the 0.2.0 diff as-is (result renamed to output, tests updated, everything green) and publish. What happens to the support board when it moves to 0.2.0?
challenges.explanation: The board stored the name result; 0.2.0 exports output; nothing maps one to the other — and the updated tests only prove the new code agrees with itself, not that old boards survive. The wizard can't save you: it validates the artifact and rejects duplicate versions, it doesn't police naming decisions. The added optional input is harmless — new pins with defaults extend the contract; renames rewrite it.

options.label: The board's stored wire into result no longer resolves — the rename is a breaking change hiding behind green tests
Nothing — Flow-Like migrates connections to the pin in the same position
The publish wizard rejects the upload because pin renames are forbidden
The new strip_punctuation input is what breaks the board — added pins invalidate saved nodes

challenges.prompt: Artifact 2: fetch_greeting calls the HTTP host service but declares no permission, and its MockHostBridge suite is green. Predict the first real board run.
challenges.explanation: Capability gates sit between the node and every protected host service; an undeclared call hits the gate and fails — ending that node's run, never the app. The mock result is the trap from the testing lesson: MockHostBridge answers whatever it's scripted to answer and never reads the permission list, so a green HTTP path proves nothing about enforcement. And consent can only grant what a node declares — this node declared nothing.

options.label: The sandbox refuses the undeclared HTTP call; the node fails safely — the app and board keep running
It works — the user consented to the package at install time, which covers HTTP
It works — the mock suite exercised the HTTP path successfully
The undeclared call crashes the executing app

challenges.prompt: Artifact 3: the 0.2.0 evidence table shows green unit tests, a green component build, and a green run in a brand-new scratch board. Which failure classes are still completely uncovered?
challenges.explanation: The scratch-board run proves the node executes once — it never reopens the board, and it carries no stored 0.1.0 identifiers, so both persistence and update compatibility remain untested. Given Artifact 1's rename, that's exactly where 0.2.0 will fail. Logic and packaging look tempting, but they're precisely what the green unit tests and green component build already cover.

options.label: A board saved under 0.1.0 failing to resolve against 0.2.0
Identifiers failing to resolve after a board is saved, closed, and reopened
A wrong changed value for a boundary input
A dependency that cannot be componentized

challenges.prompt: Artifact 4: a one-line fix, and a teammate suggests re-uploading the corrected binary as 0.1.0 'since only we installed it'. What's actually true?
challenges.explanation: Published versions are immutable by design — the backend hashes artifacts and rejects duplicate ID-version pairs, precisely so 'the same version' can never mean two different binaries. The fix ships as a new version, and because private activation is separate from public review, the team gets it immediately. The verified badge is a trust signal, not a bypass — treating it as one is the misconception worth unlearning.

options.label: The registry refuses it — a package ID plus version identifies an immutable artifact, so the fix ships as 0.1.1
The support team can move to the fixed private version without any public review
With a verified badge, administrators could hot-swap the 0.1.0 binary
Even private users must wait for publication review before using the fix

challenges.prompt: Roadmap for 0.3.0: normalize_text optionally calls a translation model, and profiling shows the package needs more memory. Where does each change land?
challenges.explanation: Same two layers as always: capabilities are exported per node in code, resource tiers bound the package in the manifest. 'Both in the manifest' is the persistent trap — a manifest permission section cannot grant a node a protected capability; users reviewing the package see the capabilities each node itself declares. The reverse split simply swaps the layers' jobs.

options.label: addPermission("models") on the node definition; a bigger memory tier in flow-like.toml
Both in flow-like.toml — permissions and limits are package concerns
Both on the node definition — everything a node needs travels with it
The models capability in the manifest; the memory tier on the node definition
